items.title: Senator Intensely Questions Cissie Graham Lynch on LGBT Views During Confirmation Hearing
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: Important.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine (D) intensely questioned Cissie Graham Lynch, the granddaughter of the late Rev. Billy Graham, on LGBT issues during her Senate confirmation hearing to serve as ambassador-at-large for international religious freedom.

Listen to the latest episode of the “Quick Start” podcast

Kaine asked Lynch, who supports a biblical understanding of marriage as a lifelong union between one male and one female, how she would work as ambassador “to protect … LGBTQ folks from persecution.” Lynch immediately responded that, in her official capacity, she would have a “responsibility to protect people of all faiths” and does not believe “anyone should ever be criminalized or persecuted for their personal beliefs.”

The senator, who identifies as Catholic, told Lynch there are “countries around the world [that] criminalize just being gay, being LGBTQ” — an interesting line of inquiry for a politician who has been intensely supportive of celebrating Islam, stating in the past that Muslim Americans “enrich the fabric of our communities,” given the religion is deeply opposed to homosexuality.

Kaine pressed Lynch to explain her view, which she expressed in February 2021, that certain LGBT nondiscrimination laws could jeopardize Christian religious freedoms, a concept that apparently was difficult for the Virginia lawmaker to understand. For context, Lynch — who has worked alongside her father, Franklin Graham, at the humanitarian organization Samaritan’s Purse — wrote in a 2021 opinion article for Fox News that the “extreme” Equality Act would “erode” religious liberties for Christians.

If enacted into law, the Equality Act, which has been introduced in Congress numerous times but has never passed through the Senate, would amend existing civil rights laws in the U.S. to explicitly prohibit any form of discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity across areas like employment, housing, and education. Lynch, for her part, has argued such legislation would override religious liberty protections, barring faith-based organizations that hold to a biblical view of sexuality from operating according to their deeply held religious convictions.

During her Senate hearing this week, Lynch specifically mentioned to Kaine the case of baker Jack Phillips, a small business owner in Denver, Colorado, who skyrocketed to national news in 2012, when he declined to make a custom wedding cake for a same-sex couple. He has faced numerous lawsuits in the years since for similar issues, all of which he has won to date.

Nevertheless, Lynch argued Phillips is a prime example of an American who has faced intense attacks because of his personally held religious beliefs when it comes to marriage. She also mentioned he has never turned away customers due to their sexual practices or personal ideologies, noting Phillips “for years” has “served people of the LGBT community” without issue.

Listen to the latest episode of the “Radical Revelations” podcast

While the ambassador-at-large nominee has her own views of sexuality and marriage, she told the senators in Congress she has always sought to engage in dialogue about these issues “with kindness” and “with respect.”

“I’ve talked about on my platform many issues that are divisive in our culture and we are in a culture that teaches us that, if we believe something differently, that we can’t get along with somebody, that that’s hate speech,” she said.

On a global scale, Lynch said she “would never be able to support something [such as a Ugandan law] where it’s criminalizing people … for their sexual identity, for their sexual preference.” She reaffirmed to Kaine she is committed, if confirmed, to “represent[ing] people of all faiths,” and drew particular attention to the religious persecution happening around the world: “People are dying. People are being persecuted. People are put into jail. There’s 80 countries with blasphemy laws.”

“I’ve learned that through my years of working when I work in the countries with people I often don’t have the same beliefs, but we come together,” she said of her humanitarian work with Samaritan’s Purse, adding her goal is to “find that common ground to help people on a bipartisan mission.”

Before a vote on Lynch’s confirmation can reach the full Senate, she must first be approved by the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, where Republicans currently hold a 12-10 majority. In the full Senate, Republicans outnumber Democrats at 53-47.

items.title: Sweeping Anti-Conversion Law Leads Indian Churches to Cancel Vacation Bible Schools
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: Whoa.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Churches in the Indian state of Maharashtra are reportedly cancelling Bible camps during Diwali, a Hindu holiday celebrated during the autumn season, because of a recently enacted anti-conversion law.

For context, Maharashtra is India’s second most-populous state and includes Mumbai, the largest city in the country. Only about 2.3% of India’s 28 million people identify as Christians, making believers an extreme minority in the nation.

Much like in the U.S., the Bible camps — vacation Bible schools — last several days and consist of music, games and competitions, and stories and lessons based on Scripture, all for children ranging in ages from five to 15 years old. In India, they typically take place in the fall, according to Premier Christian News.

Some area churches, though, have cancelled their planned VBS events altogether, while others have restricted it strictly to Christian kids — a shift from the typical strategy of using the Bible camps as opportunities to evangelize.

It all comes down to Maharashtra’s sweeping Freedom of Religion Act, signed into law by Indian President Droupadi Murmu on July 30 and enacted the following month. The language of the bill is so broad, critics are concerned it will result in the penalization of Christians and churches. The law states violators may face up to seven years in prison for the non-bailable offense.

The new law bans conversion by “allurement,” a vague and overly generalized term that includes “any temptation in the form of … any gift, gratification, easy money or material benefit either in cash or kind.” It also disallows the offer of employment, “free education in school or college run by any religious body or institution,” a “better lifestyle,” “portraying practice, rituals and ceremonies or, any integral part of a religion in a detrimental way vis-a-vis another religion,” or even “glorifying one religion” — in this case, Christianity — over another.

Additionally, anyone who intends to convert from one religion to another is required to give notice to a governmental authority 60 days prior “to such proposed conversion.” At that point, the official will announce the impending conversion to the involved parties, “calling for objections within [30] days from issuance of notice,” according to the law.

“If any objections are received or otherwise, the competent authority [government official] may make an enquiry through police with regard to the intention, purpose or cause of the proposed conversion,” the bill states, noting that, if a violation is suspected, an investigation will ensue.

According to Premier, at least 12 other states in India have similar anti-conversion laws and, while advocates argue the bills protect vulnerable people from exploitation, others see them as a clear attack on Christian evangelism. The U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom, for example, has said the laws disproportionately affect Christians and Muslims, and have noted terms like “allurement” are intentionally ambiguous and problematic.

The churches moving ahead with planned VBS initiatives are requiring registration and charging entree fees of 50 to 100 rupees (roughly $1) as a way to prove parents sent their children to these faith-based camps intentionally and of their own accord.

items.title: Sadie Robertson Huff Was the Poster Child for Christianity. She Says It Nearly Crushed Her.
items.author: Cameron Strang
items.summary: “The pressure of that felt so crippling because I wasn’t living that way,” she says of being cast as the model Christian girl on Duck Dynasty. It led to her keeping God at a distance whenever she struggled, until one night when “a freight train of God’s grace” hit her.
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

By her teens, Sadie Robertson Huff had been cast as something she never auditioned for. Huff grew up on camera, on A&E’s Duck Dynasty, in a family that lived its faith out loud, and viewers took the teenager at the center of it as the model Christian girl. She says she felt every bit of that expectation.

“I was put in this position to be this poster child for Christianity,” she said. “I’m in this Christian family. They’re all living boldly for their faith. I need to be this good example. And yet the pressure of that felt so crippling because I wasn’t living that way.”

The gap between the image and the girl got filled with performance. Huff says she kept showing viewers the version they wanted.

“Instead of just being honest and being vulnerable and being authentic and saying I struggle, I was trying to be what people were projecting on me.”

That began to change with her first YouTube video. She posted it with wet hair and no makeup, which was a bigger statement then than it sounds now, and told viewers they had it wrong.

“Hey, I’m Sadie Robertson, and here’s what my life looks like. A lot of you guys keep saying I’m goals, but I’m really struggling. I feel really insecure. I have a lot of anxiety.”

It was the first time she let the audience see the person underneath. The poster-child pressure had followed her into her prayer life, though.

“I felt like I had to be perfect for him to be proud of me. I had to be perfect to stay in right relationship. And when I wasn’t perfect, because no one is, and I definitely struggled a whole lot, then I would just distance myself from him. When you’re struggling, that’s when you need to draw near. But when I’m struggling, I’m like, ‘I gotta get it together so that I can come near.'”

The video changed how she showed up online. The private version came later, after she had kids. She was behind at work, exhausted and sure she was failing at all of it. One night, after putting the children to bed, she went outside to tell God she was sorry she just couldn’t keep up.

“I walked outside to have some quiet time, and it was like a freight train of God’s grace hit me. I had no anticipation of feeling weight lifted. I had all the anticipation for repentance. I was going to say, ‘Lord, I’m dropping the ball in every area.’ And yet I sat there and I just felt God’s embrace and I just cried. I came back in to my husband and I said, ‘That was the craziest experience. I thought He was gonna be mad at me, but He just loved me.'”

She admits it sounds hard to explain. “I can’t explain it other than it was like an embrace,” she says. “I just felt a weight lifted.” Since then she’s been on a mission to tell people that God is more gracious, more kind and more loving than they think.

Huff keeps returning to the woman at the well to explain what happened to her. She has heard John 4 preached all her life, she says, and rereading it, she noticed what the woman chose to say when she ran back to town.

“Come meet a man who told me everything I ever did. That was the testimony. And that revelation of this man knows me, and he was willing to sit with me, and he was willing to drink from my cup, that he actually loves me.”

Her new book, It’s Not Personal, is built on the same story.

The comparison has a Christian version, too. Huff says she and her husband guard against it.

“One thing as a culture we have created in the Church sometimes is that competitive spirit of who gave the best message at the conference, who did the best worship set. Christian and I are like, we cannot let our mind go there. Don’t pay that attention, because it does something to your heart. Then you’re striving. I gotta bring my best. It’s gotta be better than I was last year.”

The expectations that came with being a poster child have not gone away. Every time Huff has been in what she calls the storms of social media, she says, the criticism has come from the Church, never from the secular world. When criticism from fellow Christians piled up online, including over a TikTok dance, she dreaded the next Sunday.

“I felt nervous to go to my church, because I felt like everybody’s seen this on Facebook, everybody’s seen this on Instagram and TikTok, and I just didn’t want to feel eyes on me,” she said. “I felt sad about it, I felt hurt by it. And so Christian and I were like, ‘Hey, it’s okay. We just need to go.’

“I was trying to slip out to go help one of my kids, and one of the elders just walked up to me and said, ‘Hey, I just want to encourage you. God is using you in such a mighty way.’ He didn’t bring up the controversy. I’m sure he saw it, based off of just how kind he was being, but he just spoke so much truth in my life. And I just was thinking, I’m so grateful that I came to church.”

She says she never wants to bash the Church. She’s had hate from it and so much love, she says, and she believes in it deeply. Her request is for the people who treat the internet as a separate place.

“We all have social media. I’m seeing you react to me. I’m scrolling, it’s in my algorithm. And so don’t take the humanity out of people on the other side of the screen. It matters so much that you’re loving them just as much.”

The criticism has also followed a harder question. Huff preaches, and she didn’t grow up in a church that allowed women to. Her family wrestled with it before she said yes, she says, reading through the scriptures and asking big questions, and she is grateful they did. The comments arrive anyway.

“People comment all kinds of stuff. ‘Sit down, shut up, you are feelings based, emotion based.’ I’ve seen the comments. I’ve seen the things. But I go back to what I know to be true and what the Lord has spoken, and what I’ve read and studied and people spoke into my life. It’s hurtful, it’s sad.”

What carries her through it, she says, is something Shelley Giglio once told her.

“Life is gonna be hard, but you’re looking for assurance that it’s what the Lord told you to do. Because if you have assurance, then you’ll be able to get through the hard.”

It is a long way from the girl who believed she had to get it together before she could come near to God.

items.title: The Politics of Child Sacrifice
items.author: Dr. Matthew Petrusek
items.summary:
Dr. Matthew Petrusek

The most vulnerable and innocent among us are the perfect sacrificial victim for America’s fastest growing religion—self-worship.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Matthew Petrusek

There isn’t a politician, on the left or the right, who would publicly deny that the moral measure of a society is how it treats its most vulnerable members. 

Children are the largest group of vulnerable people. They cannot care for themselves by definition. A more specific formulation of the standard would therefore be, the moral measure of a society is how well it treats its children. 

How do we hold up?

In a word, shamefully. 

Since the end of child labor, there hasn’t been a time in our nation’s history when public policies and attitudes have been more hostile to children. It starts in the womb: Every child conceived in the United States has a 20 percent chance of being chemically or mechanically aborted. That’s one in five kids (though some stats put it closer to one in four). 

Of the 75–80 percent of children who make it past birth, about 25 percent grow up in a single-parent household, which contributes to a much higher probability that they will be sexually abused and/or neglected in ways that lead to poorer health (especially mental health), lower educational outcomes, and a much higher chance of ending up in prison. The data on this are unequivocal: Despite the strange cultural celebration of single parenthood (especially single motherhood), growing up without a mother or father in the home makes life much harder for children. 

Whatever their living situation, 90 percent of children attend public schools. Over ten percent of these students fail to make it through the twelfth grade. Of those who do graduate, roughly two‑thirds—over 60 percent—score below “proficient” in reading and math. Many then go to college where they often take on over a hundred thousand dollars of debt for, at best, questionable gains in knowledge and skill. Many more will leave high school and enter the job market functionally illiterate, all while the rise of AI scrambles the future of work itself. 

These troubling numbers correlate with economic indicators; the poorer families are, the more they tend to experience these bad outcomes. However, other policies hurt children from all economic backgrounds. For example, despite pushback from the current administration, numerous school districts still permit boys to compete in girls sports, stripping young women of awards and forcing them to share intimate changing spaces with sexually mature males. Many schools also continue to peddle the toxic lie that it is possible to be “trapped in the wrong body.” 

More generally, both public and private schools often resemble ideological training and enforcement camps rather than educational institutions. 

Progressive ideology produces many of these ills. But there’s one gaping source of harm in which both liberals and conservatives share blame: a wildly ballooning deficit that robs future generations of fiscal stability and, consequently, the conditions for economic prosperity. Social security stands closest to the budgetary cliff; the program’s reserve funds are expected to run dry within a decade. However, current deficit spending threatens every dimension of the public good for the next generations. In its current trajectory, the debt-to-GDP ratio will be 150 percent by around 2050, meaning our national debt will be 50 percent higher than the output of our entire economy. 

How will our children pay for that, especially as the cost of living continues to rise? Nobody seems to have a workable plan. 

No wonder young people have a grim view of both the present and future. In the aggregate, it’s bleak. They aren’t “blackpilling” or celebrating pessimism. They’re taking reality seriously. 
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

But none of it has to be this way. Every statistic results from a choice: parents choosing to deny their children the right to life and a stable home; schools choosing to pander to teachers’ financial interests and pet political projects rather than instructing students how to read, write, and reason (if there is any doubt well-governed public schools can still provide good education even in poor communities, just look at Mississippi’s great success); both parents and school officials cowardly submitting to the aggressively loud but numerically minuscule transgender lobby out of fear of being called a mean name; and adults from across the political spectrum engaged in childishly magical thinking that current deficit spending will somehow fix itself.

The motivations for these choices are just as craven as the choices themselves: my career, my love life; my comfort; my freedom; my plans; my free time; my fear of ostracism; my leisurely retirement; my sense of self-righteousness; my neighborhood (and to hell with the others); my benefits; my political party.

My truth. 

And who foots the bill for our collective narcissism? The most vulnerable and innocent among us, the perfect sacrificial victim for America’s fastest growing religion—self-worship. 

A version of this article also appears on the Washington Examiner.

items.author: Word on Fire
items.summary:
Word on Fire
Word on Fire hosted its fourth annual New Ressourcement Conference from November 4–6, 2026. The theme was “Joseph Ratzinger and His Sources,” in honor of the upcoming centenary of Ratzinger’s birth (April 16, 2027). Scholars were invited to share papers reflecting on the minds and texts
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Word on Fire

Word on Fire hosted its fourth annual New Ressourcement Conference from November 4–6, 2026. The theme was “Joseph Ratzinger and His Sources,” in honor of the upcoming centenary of Ratzinger’s birth (April 16, 2027). Scholars were invited to share papers reflecting on the minds and texts that shaped Ratzinger’s writing. 

“Joseph Ratzinger’s theology grew out of a lifetime of reading: Scripture and the liturgy, Augustine and Bonaventure, and the friends, teachers, and opponents he engaged along the way. This year’s conference brought scholars together to study those sources and to ask what they still offer the Church,” said Dr. Jason Paone, director of Word on Fire Academic. “With the centenary of his birth approaching and the inaugural volume of his Collected Works now available in English, this is a good moment to read Ratzinger the way he read the tradition, by going back to the sources.”

The conference included several keynote speakers:

  • Bishop Robert Barron, Diocese of Winona-Rochester: “The Necessity of a Metaphysics of Logos in the Determination of Justice: An Examination of the Ratzinger-Habermas Debate.”
  • Tracey Rowland, University of Notre Dame Australia: “Gottlieb Söhngen: Champion of the Analogia Fidei and its Critical Concepts.”
  • Cyril O’Regan, University of Notre Dame: “Benedict’s Sources: Imitation, Emulation, Figuration.”

The eight plenary speakers were Jennifer N. Martin (University of Notre Dame), Christopher Ruddy (Catholic University of America), Fr. Aaron Pidel (Pontifical Gregorian University), Fr. Maurice Ashley Agbaw-Ebai (Angelicum), Nina Heereman (St. Patrick’s Seminary and University), Fr. Emery de Gaál (University of Saint Mary of the Lake), Pietro Luca Azzaro (Fondazione Ratzinger), and Alejandro Sada (Universidad Panamericana). 

Throughout the conference, more than forty additional papers were shared during concurrent sessions on Scripture, liturgy and the sacraments, the Church Fathers, Bonaventure, philosophy, and Protestant theology.

Select essays will be published in the Fall 2027 special issue of The New Ressourcement journal, guest-edited by Tracey Rowland and Fr. Maurice Agbaw-Ebai.

The conference opened two days after Word on Fire Academic launched Jesus of Nazareth, the inaugural volume of the Joseph Ratzinger: Collected Works, the English edition of his non-magisterial writings.

The fifth annual New Ressourcement Conference will take place from November 16–19, 2027, at The Catholic University of America in Washington, DC. The theme will be announced in the coming months.
